title: Backtracking: Managing State in a Decision Tree
summary: Separate the current path, candidate range, and undo operations to make recursive search understandable.

sections.heading: Understanding the problem and boundaries
paragraphs: Backtracking enumerates solutions that satisfy constraints: combinations ask which elements to choose, permutations ask in what order to arrange them, and partitioning asks where to place boundaries. Draw one level of decisions before writing recursion. A tree node represents choices already made, and an edge represents a new choice. Leaves are not necessarily valid answers: specify when to collect results and which nodes can no longer lead to a complete solution.

sections.heading: Choices and invariants
paragraphs: A recursive function should describe one state: the current path and the choices still available. On entry, the path must satisfy the constraints for the portion already processed. Add one element to the path, then pass the candidate range to the next level. After recursion returns, restore the path and related markers so the next sibling branch begins from the same parent state.

sections.heading: Search process and correctness
paragraphs: Combinations use increasing indices to eliminate duplicates caused by ordering; permutations use usage markers to place each item only once; partitioning uses a start position to ensure segments cover the input continuously. Pruning requires justification: for example, stop when too few elements remain to complete a combination. Skipping a choice simply because it currently looks poor can remove correct answers as well.

For debugging, print recursion depth, the current path, and the next starting position to observe the edge corresponding to each choice. If a parent’s second branch inherits markers from its first branch, restoration is incomplete. First make the version without pruning correct, then add individually justified filters and compare the resulting answer sets.

sections.heading: Python implementation and tradeoffs
paragraphs: The template below enumerates combinations of k indices. Each path.append is paired with path.pop. Copy the path when collecting it so later changes do not alter lists already stored in the result. Answer length determines recursion depth; visited search nodes and answer copying determine most of the running time. When the function finishes, path should be empty again, a useful check for leaked state.

time: O(Σ(d=0..k) C(n,d) + k·C(n,k)), including answer copying
space: O(k) for recursion and the path; O(k·C(n,k)) for output

walkthrough: The root first chooses 0; the next level may choose only 1 or 2.
After undoing 0, choose 1; only 2 can follow.

pitfalls: Do not place the mutable path itself directly into the results.
State restoration must include usage markers or the board as well as the path.

title: 77. Combinations: Start with the Complete Search Tree
summary: Advance the next starting position so every unordered combination appears once.

sections.heading: Understanding the problem and boundaries
paragraphs: Choose k distinct integers from 1 through n. Only membership matters, not order: [1,3] and [3,1] are the same combination. To make output unique, require the path to be strictly increasing. This chooses a canonical representation for each unordered set rather than imposing an additional restriction. For k=0, there is one empty combination; for k>n, there is no solution.

sections.heading: Choices and invariants
paragraphs: The recursive state consists of start and path. Values in path have been chosen in increasing order, and start is the smallest currently available value. After adding i, the next level starts at i+1, so it can neither reuse i nor return to a smaller number. A single starting position thus prevents reuse and eliminates duplicates caused by ordering.

sections.heading: Search process and correctness
paragraphs: Once the path length equals k, collect it and return immediately; going farther would only produce paths that are too long. Otherwise, try every number from start through n. Every valid combination has a smallest element, and that element’s branch can then choose the second smallest, so no combination is omitted. Branches also differ in their first choice, ensuring distinct results.

For k=2, each root candidate determines the first item in a combination, and each second-level candidate determines the second item. Use this small example to check the meaning of start, then generalize to deeper levels without writing a separate loop for every level.

sections.heading: Python implementation and tradeoffs
paragraphs: The baseline deliberately retains branches with too few remaining elements so the complete search is visible. The for loop ends at n+1 because Python range excludes its right endpoint. Store path.copy() in the results, and execute pop after recursion returns. Distinguish space for the current path from space for all results; output is often much larger than the search stack.

time: O(Σ(d=0..k) C(n,d) + k·C(n,k)); invalid k returns immediately
space: O(k) auxiliary search space; O(k·C(n,k)) output

walkthrough: After choosing 1, try only 2, 3, and 4.
When the root chooses 4, no second number is available, so that branch ends naturally.

pitfalls: Starting the next level at i reuses the same number.
This code has no pruning based on the remaining count; complexity cannot count only valid answers.

title: 77. Combinations: Pruning by the Remaining Count
summary: Derive the loop’s upper bound from the number of choices still needed to eliminate branches that cannot be completed.

sections.heading: Understanding the problem and boundaries
paragraphs: The combination baseline visits many nodes that must fail. For example, when choosing 3 numbers from 1 through 5, choosing 4 first already leaves too few later numbers. This section preserves the definition of combinations and the output order, changing only the candidate loop’s upper bound. Understanding this bound matters more than memorizing its formula, because the same reasoning applies to fixed-length strings and partitioning tasks.

sections.heading: Choices and invariants
paragraphs: Suppose d numbers have already been chosen and need=k-d remain. If the next choice is x, at least need-1 larger numbers must remain afterward. There are n-x numbers from x+1 through n, so n-x≥need-1, or x≤n-need+1. This is a necessary condition, so removing candidates that violate it cannot remove correct answers.

sections.heading: Search process and correctness
paragraphs: At each level, iterate only from start through last, where last=n-need+1. Return first if the path already has length k; no candidates need to be computed then. The path remains strictly increasing, and the baseline’s completeness and uniqueness arguments still apply: the next item of every valid combination satisfies the remaining-count condition, so its entire search path survives.

sections.heading: Python implementation and tradeoffs
paragraphs: Python range(start,last+1) converts the inclusive inequality into a half-open range. Do not write last as n-k+1, because need changes with recursion depth. Pruning reduces visited nodes, but enumerating all answers still has an output lower bound. Copying each result takes k elements, so total time cannot be O(k).

time: O(k·C(n,k)) for 1≤k≤n; O(1) when k=0
space: O(k) auxiliary search space; O(k·C(n,k)) output

example.output: 10 combinations in total; the first is [1,2,3] and the last is [3,4,5]
walkthrough: At the root, need=3 and the largest candidate is 3.
After choosing 3, need=2, and the next level can start only at 4.

pitfalls: Update the upper bound with the current path length.
Pruning removes invalid branches but cannot avoid the cost of outputting every combination.

title: 216. Combination Sum III
summary: Use the remaining count and minimum and maximum achievable sums together to decide whether a branch can succeed.

sections.heading: Understanding the problem and boundaries
paragraphs: Use only numbers 1 through 9, each at most once, to choose exactly k numbers whose sum is n. This adds a sum constraint to ordinary combinations and a count constraint to reusable combination sum. Build the path in increasing order so the same group of numbers cannot appear multiple times in different orders. Collect a result only when both its length and sum are correct.

sections.heading: Choices and invariants
paragraphs: Pass start and remain to recursion: remain is the sum still needed, and need is the number of missing numbers. The smallest achievable sum uses need consecutive numbers starting at start; the largest uses the need largest numbers, 9, 8, and so on. If too few candidates remain or remain lies outside these bounds, the branch has no solution.

sections.heading: Search process and correctness
paragraphs: When need=0, check whether remain is zero. Otherwise, check the bounds first, then try numbers x in increasing order. All numbers are positive, so if x>remain, all later, larger numbers are unusable too, and the loop can stop. Each recursive step decreases both the remaining count and the remaining sum, keeping the constraints consistent at every node.

sections.heading: Python implementation and tradeoffs
paragraphs: Arithmetic-series formulas avoid allocating temporary lists for pruning: min_sum=need*(2*start+need-1)//2 and max_sum=need*(19-need)//2. These formulas assume candidates are fixed at 1 through 9 and cannot be transferred directly to an arbitrary input array. Store copies in the output; if k is outside 0 through 9, return an empty list immediately.

time: O(Σ(d=0..k) C(9,d)+k·C(9,k)), usually less after pruning
space: O(k) auxiliary search space, excluding results

walkthrough: After choosing 1, two numbers with sum 8 are still needed.
After [1,2], the final number must be 6; after [1,3], it must be 5.

pitfalls: Do not collect a path that reaches the target sum with too few numbers.
Both maximum-sum and minimum-sum pruning require enough candidates to remain.

title: 17. Letter Combinations of a Phone Number
summary: Each level handles one digit, so input length naturally determines result length.

sections.heading: Understanding the problem and boundaries
paragraphs: Given a digit string containing only 2 through 9, choose one keypad letter for each digit and return all possible strings. Positions make independent choices even when their digits match: 22 produces aa and ab, for example. This is a Cartesian product of candidate sets rather than choosing several elements from one shared set, so neither start nor used is needed.

sections.heading: Choices and invariants
paragraphs: The recursive index pos is the number of digits already processed, and path always has length pos. Level pos may choose only letters mapped from digits[pos], then proceeds to pos+1. This invariant makes termination direct: when pos reaches input length, the path contains exactly one letter for every digit.

sections.heading: Search process and correctness
paragraphs: For any valid result, its first letter corresponds to one edge from the root, and each later position corresponds to another edge, so the search must visit it. Conversely, every path reaching the end chooses one letter from each mapping and is therefore valid. Candidate sets at different levels are independent; there are no reordered duplicates to remove.

A digit 7 or 9 provides four candidates, while every other digit provides three. The result count must equal the product of these counts. This gives an independent check: count the results, then check each string’s length and whether each position belongs to the appropriate mapping.

sections.heading: Python implementation and tradeoffs
paragraphs: Store characters in a list and execute ''.join(path) at each leaf to avoid repeatedly concatenating long strings during recursion. By this problem’s convention, empty input returns an empty list rather than a list containing the empty string. The sample implementation explicitly rejects 0, 1, and other characters, distinguishing invalid input from valid input with no results.

time: O(m·P), where m is the digit count and P is the product of the letter counts at all positions
space: O(m) auxiliary search space; O(m·P) results

walkthrough: Choose a at the first level, then d, e, and f in turn at the second.
Undo a, choose b at the first level, and repeat the second-level choices.

pitfalls: Match the problem’s convention for empty input.
Do not reuse the first digit’s candidate set at every level.

title: 39. Combination Sum: Reusing Candidates
summary: Recurse from the current index to permit reuse; nondecreasing indices eliminate duplicates caused by ordering.

sections.heading: Understanding the problem and boundaries
paragraphs: Given distinct positive integers candidates, each of which may be used any number of times, find combinations summing to target. Positivity is essential for termination and pruning. A reusable zero prevents recursion from making progress, while negative numbers mean exceeding the target does not prove the remaining branch impossible. The implementation below explicitly validates positivity and sorts candidates.

sections.heading: Choices and invariants
paragraphs: The state start is the smallest index still available, and remain is the sum still needed. After choosing nums[i], the next level still starts at i, allowing the current value to be reused. It never returns to a smaller index, so each combination appears only in nondecreasing order. The sum of path plus remain always equals the initial target.

sections.heading: Search process and correctness
paragraphs: Save an answer when remain=0. While scanning candidates, break if the current value exceeds remain, since all later values are at least as large. Each recursive step decreases remain by at least the smallest candidate, guaranteeing termination. Every valid nondecreasing combination can follow its corresponding indices one item at a time, ensuring completeness and uniqueness.

For example, with only candidate 2 and target 5, the remaining sum eventually becomes 1. No candidate is then usable, and the branch returns naturally. Search need not select an element at every level: an unsatisfiable node simply finishes its loop. Only nodes with zero remaining sum contribute answers.

sections.heading: Python implementation and tradeoffs
paragraphs: The example creates a new sorted candidate list to preserve the caller’s data. set merges duplicate candidates because equal values have no separate identity in this problem. target=0 returns one empty combination, matching the mathematical convention of choosing zero numbers. Time depends on the target and smallest candidate, so a polynomial bound cannot be given from candidates length alone.

time: O(m log m) sorting; conservative search bound O((m+1)^D·(D+1)), with D=floor(target/min(nums))
space: O(m+D) auxiliary space, excluding output; D=0 with no candidates

walkthrough: After choosing 2 twice, remain=3.
Choosing 3 completes an answer; choosing 7 also directly reduces the remaining sum to zero.

pitfalls: When reuse is allowed, recurse from i rather than i+1.
The positivity assumption is essential; this algorithm does not apply to inputs containing zero or negative numbers.

title: 40. Combination Sum II: Skipping Equal Values at the Same Level
summary: Separate element identity from answer values: deduplicate within a level and advance one index for the next level.

sections.heading: Understanding the problem and boundaries
paragraphs: The array may contain duplicate values, but each array position may be used at most once, and output value combinations must be distinct. Two cards valued 1 may be used together to form [1,1], but choosing either card as a single 1 must not produce duplicate answers. Sorting puts these equivalent choices next to each other for comparison.

sections.heading: Choices and invariants
paragraphs: The state start prevents indices from moving backward. After choosing i, recurse from i+1 so each position is used at most once. The condition i>start and nums[i]==nums[i-1] skips duplicate candidates only at the current level. When i==start, a value equal to one from the previous level remains allowed, preserving valid combinations such as [1,1].

sections.heading: Search process and correctness
paragraphs: The first occurrence of an equal value at a level already represents every solution beginning with that value. Starting instead at a later equal occurrence only repeats solutions or reduces available positions; it cannot create new value combinations. Collect when remain=0 and stop the loop when the candidate exceeds remain. Positive input ensures the remaining sum decreases and makes break valid.

Consider [1,1,2] with target 2. Choosing the first 1 at the root still permits the second 1 at the next level, producing [1,1]. The root skips its second 1, while 2 independently produces [2]. This example checks both usage limits and the scope of deduplication.

sections.heading: Python implementation and tradeoffs
paragraphs: Do not convert nums to a set beforehand: duplicate counts determine whether some combinations exist. Obtain a copy with sorted, then validate that all candidates are positive. Write both parts of the deduplication condition explicitly so it is clear that it compares sibling branches rather than forbidding equal adjacent values on a path.

time: O(n log n+n·2^n) conservative upper bound, including result copying
space: O(n) for search and the sorted copy, excluding output

walkthrough: Keep the first 1 at the root and skip the second 1 as a sibling branch.
Inside the next level after the first 1, the second 1 is that level’s starting candidate and may be chosen.

pitfalls: A global set cannot replace the array in this problem.
Using i>0 for deduplication incorrectly removes repeated numbers needed across different levels.

title: 131. Palindrome Partitioning
summary: Precompute palindromic intervals, then enumerate valid next segments starting at the current position.

sections.heading: Understanding the problem and boundaries
paragraphs: Split the entire string into nonempty segments, each of which must be a palindrome, and return every partition. Preserve character order; characters cannot be rearranged. Each decision selects the next segment’s ending position. For aab, the first segment can be a or aa, but aab itself is not a palindrome and cannot be taken as a complete solution.

sections.heading: Choices and invariants
paragraphs: The recursive start means the prefix s[:start] has already been validly partitioned, with its segments stored in path. Try every end≥start, continuing only when s[start:end+1] is a palindrome. To avoid repeatedly scanning the same interval, let pal[i][j] record whether the closed interval is palindromic, determined by matching endpoints and a palindromic interior.

sections.heading: Search process and correctness
paragraphs: Precompute with i moving right to left, ensuring pal[i+1][j-1] is ready when needed. For intervals of length one or two, compare endpoints only. At start=n, the whole string has been covered, so collect immediately. Each partition has a unique boundary sequence, and the loop enumerates every possible boundary, giving neither omissions nor duplicates.

For aaaa, every nonempty contiguous segment is palindromic, and every gap between adjacent characters may either be cut or left intact. Output therefore reaches its worst-case exponential size. Precomputation optimizes repeated validation but cannot reduce enumeration of every partition to polynomial time.

sections.heading: Python implementation and tradeoffs
paragraphs: Python string slices copy characters, so recursion count alone does not capture the cost. Precomputation uses an O(n²) Boolean table. The segments in each output partition contain n characters in total, and there can be 2^(n-1) partitions. This general implementation treats the empty string as having one empty partition; if the problem guarantees nonempty input, that case merely completes the interface.

time: O(n²+n·2^n) worst case, including string slicing and output
space: O(n²) palindrome table plus O(n) search stack, excluding output

walkthrough: With a as the first segment, the remaining ab must be split into a and b.
With aa as the first segment, the remaining b is itself a palindrome.

pitfalls: The next partitioning level must start at end+1.
Do not create the Boolean table with [[False]*n]*n, which shares rows.

title: 93. Restore IP Addresses
summary: Bound the remaining character count by the remaining segment count, then validate each numeric segment’s format.

sections.heading: Understanding the problem and boundaries
paragraphs: Split a digit string into four segments, each valued from 0 through 255, with no leading zero in a multi-digit segment. Use every character without deleting or reordering any. Validity includes format as well as numeric range: 00 has numeric value zero but is invalid, while a segment consisting only of 0 is valid.

sections.heading: Choices and invariants
paragraphs: The state start is the next segment’s beginning, and path length is the number of segments already formed. If parts=4-len(path) segments remain, the remaining character count must lie between parts and 3*parts, since each segment uses one to three digits. This count constraint eliminates many impossible branches before specific segments are tried.

sections.heading: Search process and correctness
paragraphs: At each level, try next-segment lengths one through three. Stop upon encountering a multi-digit segment beginning with 0, since longer segments retain the same problem. Also stop when its value exceeds 255: a longer nonnegative decimal number cannot become smaller. Output only when all four segments are complete and all characters are consumed; both conditions must hold.

An input of length 13 can stop at the root: even four three-digit segments cover only twelve digits. For 010010, the first segment must be 0; reject 01 before recursion because it violates formatting. Such boundary cases expose errors more effectively than ordinary addresses alone.

sections.heading: Python implementation and tradeoffs
paragraphs: Keep segments as strings and join them with periods at the end, preserving formatting information that numeric conversion would discard. int validates range only and cannot replace the leading-zero check. Return an empty list if input contains nondigits. Four segments of at most three digits impose a small absolute bound on the candidate count; do not describe it as exponential search growing arbitrarily with string length.

time: O(n+3^4), where n is input length; valid lengths are only 4..12
space: O(4) auxiliary search space, excluding output

walkthrough: The length constraint forces the first two segments to be the three-digit 255.
Split the remaining 11135 into 11|135 or 111|35.

pitfalls: Do not check numeric value while ignoring leading zeros.
Do not output four segments if characters remain.

title: 78. Subsets: Every Node Represents an Answer
summary: A valid current path is already a subset; there is no need to wait for a leaf.

sections.heading: Understanding the problem and boundaries
paragraphs: Given distinct integers, return all subsets, including the empty set and the full set. Subset length is unrestricted, so the combination rule of collecting only at length k does not apply. Require increasing element indices, and each path corresponds uniquely to a subset; path length is simply that subset’s size.

sections.heading: Choices and invariants
paragraphs: The state start restricts subsequent choices to that index or later positions, and path represents the current subset. Save path on every recursive entry: whether or not it can be extended, it is already valid. Then choose a later element and move the starting position to i+1, preventing reuse and duplicates caused by ordering.

sections.heading: Search process and correctness
paragraphs: The root’s empty path contributes the empty set. Every nonempty subset has a unique smallest index, chosen in its corresponding branch, after which later recursion adds the remaining indices. Collecting every node instead of only leaves covers subsets of every size without separately running combinations for different k values.

The subset [2] need not be represented by a leaf at a fixed depth. It is the node reached when the root selects the second item. Recording it immediately preserves [2] while still allowing the next level to generate larger subsets such as [2,3].

sections.heading: Python implementation and tradeoffs
paragraphs: Copy the path into results. Input needs no sorting because distinct values are guaranteed, and original index order already provides a unique representation. There are 2^n subsets of n elements, with n·2^(n-1) elements across all outputs, so O(n·2^n) time and output size are natural. The current path and recursion stack need only O(n).

time: O(n·2^n); O(1) when n=0
space: O(n) auxiliary space; O(n·2^n) output

walkthrough: First record [] at the root.
Choose 1 and record [1], then choose 2 and record [1,2]; finally choose 2 at the root.

pitfalls: Collecting only at the end misses many shorter subsets.
Deduplication here depends on input values being distinct.

title: 90. Subsets II: Skip Duplicate Values Only at the Same Level
summary: After sorting, skip equivalent sibling branches while retaining repeated values on a single path.

sections.heading: Understanding the problem and boundaries
paragraphs: The array may contain duplicate integers; subsets are compared by value and must be unique. For [1,2,2], both [2] and [2,2] are allowed, but choosing either individual 2 position must produce only one [2]. Sort to place equal values next to each other, then use the current level’s start to distinguish duplicate branches from valid repeated members.

sections.heading: Choices and invariants
paragraphs: Each node first collects its current path, then tries later indices. If i>start and nums[i]==nums[i-1], that value has already been tried at this level, so skip it. After choosing the first 2, the next level may choose the second 2: it is exactly the new level’s start and does not satisfy the skip condition.

sections.heading: Search process and correctness
paragraphs: Why does keeping only the first equal value at each level suffice? Its position is earliest, so it has at least as many equal elements available afterward as any later occurrence. Every possible repetition count can therefore be built starting from it. Skipping later positions removes duplicate representations without losing subsets such as [2,2] that need multiple equal elements.

For an array containing three 2s, the only distinct value subsets are [], [2], [2,2], and [2,2,2]. Search keeps one equal-valued starting choice per level while allowing remaining positions at deeper levels. This example clearly shows why deduplication reduces the node count.

sections.heading: Python implementation and tradeoffs
paragraphs: The code uses sorted(nums) to preserve caller input. A global set that removes input duplicates discards counts that form part of the answer. Likewise, forbidding additions with path[-1]==nums[i] removes valid repeated members outright. Output count is at most 2^n and is smaller with many duplicates, but worst-case analysis still uses distinct input values.

time: O(n log n+n·2^n) worst case
space: O(n) auxiliary space, excluding output

walkthrough: Under [1], choose the first 2, then enter the next level and choose the other 2.
Back at the same level under [1], skip the second 2.

pitfalls: Apply the deduplication restriction only to sibling branches.
Converting input to a set loses duplicate counts.

title: 491. Nondecreasing Subsequences: Do Not Sort the Input
summary: Preserve original order and use a separate set at each level to eliminate equal candidate values.

sections.heading: Understanding the problem and boundaries
paragraphs: Find nondecreasing subsequences of length at least two. Elements need not be contiguous, but must retain their order in the original array. Nondecreasing permits equal adjacent values. Unlike Subsets II, sorting changes which elements can precede others and therefore changes the problem itself; do not sort and apply the adjacent-value deduplication formula.

sections.heading: Choices and invariants
paragraphs: The state start restricts later elements to positions after the current one, and the final value in path supplies the nondecreasing threshold. A smaller nums[i] cannot be added. Create a new seen set for every recursive call to record values already tried at that level and prevent equivalent sibling branches. Sets at different levels must remain independent.

sections.heading: Search process and correctness
paragraphs: The earliest occurrence of a value at a level has the most subsequent candidates. Choosing a later occurrence of the same value cannot create additional value sequences, so skipping duplicates at that level is safe. Record a path as soon as its length reaches two, then keep extending it to include both short and long sequences. Recurse from i+1 to preserve original order.

For [7,4,7], globally forbidding the final 7 because 7 has already been seen would lose [7,7]. The final 7 competes with the first 7 at the root, but is a valid extension at the next level after choosing the first 7.

sections.heading: Python implementation and tradeoffs
paragraphs: seen records neither every element ever visited nor the values already in the current path. Reusing it globally incorrectly removes valid results. The code calls seen.add after validity checks, making it explicit that the set records only candidates actually expanded. Negative numbers do not affect the comparison logic. Search remains exponential in the worst case; include output copying and per-level sets in the analysis.

time: O(n·2^n) worst case, including candidate scans and answer copying
space: O(n²) conservative auxiliary bound for seen sets across recursive levels, plus O(n) for the path

walkthrough: After choosing the first 7 at the root, the next level may still choose the second 7.
When the root encounters 7 again, its current-level seen already contains 7, so skip the equivalent branch.

pitfalls: Sorting input destroys the subsequence’s original order.
Create a new seen inside every dfs call.

title: 46. Permutations: Tracking Used Indices
summary: Every permutation level chooses from all elements; used prevents reusing an input position.

sections.heading: Understanding the problem and boundaries
paragraphs: Given distinct integers, return every permutation. Combinations can eliminate ordering through increasing indices, but permutations must retain both [1,2] and [2,1], so the next level cannot start at i+1. Each input element is used exactly once in a complete path, and its position in the path is its position in the permutation.

sections.heading: Choices and invariants
paragraphs: used[i] records whether the ith input element is already in the current permutation. On entering recursion at depth d, path has length d and used has exactly d true entries, corresponding one-to-one to path elements. Every level scans all indices, skips used elements, and may choose any remaining index as its next item.

sections.heading: Search process and correctness
paragraphs: At path length n, every element has been used exactly once, so collect and return. The first, second, and later items of any permutation can be chosen at their corresponding levels, making search complete. Distinct input elements make different choice sequences yield different results. After recursion, undo both path and used so earlier choices do not contaminate sibling branches.

used refers to indices rather than values, separating element identity from its current position. The index-based framework is unchanged for strings or other comparable objects. Equal element values, however, require additional permutation deduplication; Boolean usage markers do not automatically eliminate identical results.

sections.heading: Python implementation and tradeoffs
paragraphs: This example uses a Boolean array instead of searching with x in path, making usage checks constant time. Length-zero input produces one empty permutation, useful as a building block for other algorithms. There are n! results, each copying n items, so time is O(n·n!). used, the path, and the recursion stack need only linear auxiliary space.

code:
def solve(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    used = [False] * n
    ans, path = [], []
    def dfs():
        if len(path) == n:
            ans.append(path.copy())
            return
        for i in range(n):
            if used[i]:
                continue
            used[i] = True
            path.append(nums[i])
            dfs()
            path.pop()
            used[i] = False
    dfs()
    return ans
time: O(n·n!); O(1) when n=0
space: O(n) auxiliary space; O(n·n!) output

walkthrough: After choosing 1 for the first position, the second may choose 2 or 3.
Back at the root, undo 1; the next major branch may start with 2.

pitfalls: Permutations cannot restrict candidates with an increasing start.
Forgetting to undo used makes later branches miss answers.

title: 47. Permutations II: Distinguishing Levels from Branches
summary: After sorting, require equal elements to enter the path in index order, avoiding duplicates from swapping equal elements.

sections.heading: Understanding the problem and boundaries
paragraphs: Input may contain duplicate values; return all distinct permutations. Different positions with equal values have separate uses, but swapping them produces no new answer. For example, [1,1,2] has three permutations. Treating the two 1s as labeled objects creates six leaf paths, whose equivalent representations must be eliminated.

sections.heading: Choices and invariants
paragraphs: Sort first and retain the used array. Skip candidate i if it has already been used. Also skip it if nums[i]==nums[i-1] and the previous position has not been used. This requires equal values to enter the path in original index order. When the previous position is already in the current path, adding the later equal value is entirely valid.

sections.heading: Search process and correctness
paragraphs: Two equal values at the same level generate the same subsequent value permutations, so the earliest unused position suffices as their representative. More intuitively, every value permutation has a unique assignment of its first 1 to the first input 1, its second 1 to the second input 1, and so on. This canonical assignment preserves exactly one search path.

Running [1,1] alone should yield just [1,1]. The first level rejects starting with the second 1, and the next level permits it after the first. This preserves both available uses while eliminating duplicates from exchanging the cards’ identities.

sections.heading: Python implementation and tradeoffs
paragraphs: This deduplication condition differs from i>start in combinations because permutations have no increasing starting position. not used[i-1] asks whether the previous equal element is still competing at this level. Reversing it may yield another search strategy, but changes the proof and search efficiency. When learning, retain this consistent invariant.

code:
def solve(nums):
    nums = sorted(nums)
    n = len(nums)
    used = [False] * n
    ans, path = [], []
    def dfs():
        if len(path) == n:
            ans.append(path.copy())
            return
        for i in range(n):
            if used[i]:
                continue
            if i > 0 and nums[i] == nums[i - 1] and not used[i - 1]:
                continue
            used[i] = True
            path.append(nums[i])
            dfs()
            path.pop()
            used[i] = False
    dfs()
    return ans

space: O(n) auxiliary space, excluding output

title: Deduplication: Per-Level Sets and Adjacent Comparisons After Sorting
summary: Deduplication eliminates equivalent candidate branches; sorting and sets are two ways to express that equivalence.

sections.heading: Problem and applicability
paragraphs: Duplicate answers often arise when different indices with the same value generate identical continuations at one level. If input order has no meaning, sort to place duplicates together, then test i>start and equality with the preceding item. If input order determines answers, as in nondecreasing subsequences, preserve it and use a per-level set to record values already tried.

sections.heading: State and key invariants
paragraphs: Both functions below generate distinct subsets so their mechanisms can be compared. The sorted version builds canonical nondecreasing paths. The set version preserves original index order, so it cannot claim unique value subsets for arbitrary unsorted duplicate input: [1,2,1], for example, produces both [1,2] and [2,1]. For a fair comparison, the set version in this example also sorts first.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: A new set is created in each recursive call and constrains only sibling branches of that node; repeated values along a path remain allowed. Adjacent comparisons after sorting implicitly encode whether this level has already chosen a value through the loop index. The mechanisms are equivalent in essence, but sets need extra hash storage, while sorted comparisons require equal values to be adjacent.

Compare actual value sequences and duplicates, not just the final counts from the two methods. If the set version preserves original order for a subsequence problem, reanalyze it together with nondecreasing or other validity constraints. Equivalence for sorted subsets does not automatically extend to order-sensitive problems.

sections.heading: Implementation details and decisions
paragraphs: First ask whether input may be reordered, then whether duplicates represent separate available uses. A set must not globally remove duplicate inputs beforehand, which would lose [2,2]. If output order also carries meaning, the set version is not a universal deduplication tool: prove again that equal candidates represent identical subsequent answers.

code:
def subsets_sorted(nums):
    nums = sorted(nums)
    ans, path = [], []
    def dfs(start):
        ans.append(path.copy())
        for i in range(start, len(nums)):
            if i > start and nums[i] == nums[i - 1]:
                continue
            path.append(nums[i])
            dfs(i + 1)
            path.pop()
    dfs(0)
    return ans

def subsets_layer_set(nums):
    nums = sorted(nums)
    ans, path = [], []
    def dfs(start):
        ans.append(path.copy())
        seen = set()
        for i in range(start, len(nums)):
            if nums[i] in seen:
                continue
            seen.add(nums[i])
            path.append(nums[i])
            dfs(i + 1)
            path.pop()
    dfs(0)
    return ans
time: Both have worst-case O(n log n+n·2^n) time
space: O(n) auxiliary space for sorted comparisons; conservative O(n²) for per-level sets, excluding results

After choosing the first 2, the new level may still choose the second.

A per-level set is not global removal of duplicate values.

title: 332. Reconstruct Itinerary: Building an Eulerian Path in Reverse
summary: Consume edges first and append an airport only when no continuation remains, keeping small dead ends out of the route’s front.

sections.heading: Problem and applicability
paragraphs: Each ticket is a directed edge. Start at JFK, use every ticket exactly once, and select the lexicographically smallest feasible itinerary. Airports may appear repeatedly, and duplicate tickets are distinct edges. A visited set of airports is therefore unsuitable: edges are what must be consumed. The problem normally guarantees an itinerary using all tickets.

sections.heading: State and key invariants
paragraphs: This is an Eulerian path in a directed graph. Sort each airport’s destinations in reverse order so popping the last item yields its lexicographically smallest remaining edge. Follow edges until no continuation remains, append the airport to route, and backtrack. These records are in completion order rather than departure order; reverse them to obtain the itinerary. Dead ends naturally settle at the end.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: An iterative stack simulates Hierholzer’s algorithm. If its top has an outgoing edge, push that destination; otherwise, pop the airport into the reversed answer. Later-discovered circuits are inserted at their matching positions in the earlier route, connecting every consumed edge into a complete path. Exploring smaller destinations first gives the lexicographically smallest feasible splicing when an Eulerian path exists.

If KUL is immediately recorded as the second stop from JFK, travel gets stuck and leaves two tickets unused. Reverse construction can explore this terminal airport first while reserving it for the end. This counterexample shows that lexicographic choices must be combined with the global structure required to use every edge.

sections.heading: Implementation details and decisions
paragraphs: Checking result length alone does not validate itineraries for arbitrary invalid input. Without Eulerian conditions, adjacent airports after reversal may not correspond to tickets. This implementation additionally uses Counter to verify usage counts for every adjacent edge and returns an empty list if validation fails. An iterative stack avoids Python recursion-depth limits, and adjacency lists naturally preserve parallel edges.

space: O(E+V), including adjacency lists, the stack, and edge counts

walkthrough: Explore KUL first. With no outgoing edges, it is added first to the reversed result.
Then explore NRT→JFK; after reversal, KUL becomes the final stop.

pitfalls: Immediately outputting the smallest destination can prevent using remaining tickets.
Do not globally mark airports visited; edges are the units consumed.
Do not convert parallel edges to a set before sorting.

title: 51. N-Queens: Row-by-Row Search and Diagonal Identifiers
summary: Place one queen per row and check conflicts with column and two diagonal sets.

sections.heading: Problem and applicability
paragraphs: Place n queens on an n×n board so no two share a row, column, or diagonal, and return every board. Recursing row by row places exactly one queen per level and automatically eliminates same-row conflicts. Only columns and the two diagonal directions remain to manage; there is no need to scan the whole board against all placed queens for each attempt.

sections.heading: State and key invariants
paragraphs: One diagonal family through (r,c) shares r-c; the other shares r+c. cols, diag_down, and diag_up store occupied column and diagonal identifiers. On entering level r, these three sets describe exactly the queens in the first r rows. Item i in the positions list is the queen’s column in row i.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: Try each column. If none of its three identifiers is occupied, update state and recurse to the next row. On return from a failed branch, undo all three sets and the position list. At r=n, every row contains a queen, and each insertion passed the conflict check, so the board is valid. Every valid board likewise corresponds to a unique row-by-row sequence of column choices.

Neither n=2 nor n=3 has a solution; search backtracks completely to the root and returns an empty list. n=1 has one solution, useful for checking board-string generation. For n=4, independently validate output by reading the queen’s column in each row and checking that columns and both diagonal identifiers have no duplicates.

sections.heading: Implementation details and decisions
paragraphs: Store search state as a position list and generate strings of Qs and periods only when a solution is found, reducing board copying in invalid branches. r-c may be negative; sets support negative integers without any offset. This implementation gives one empty-board solution for n=0 and no results for negative n. Generating each complete board costs O(n²) characters.

space: O(n) auxiliary search space; O(S·n²) output

The column sequence [1,3,0,2] generates a complete board.

The two diagonal families use difference and sum identifiers, respectively.

title: 37. Sudoku Solver: Choose the Empty Cell with the Fewest Candidates
summary: Maintain row, column, and box constraints, prioritizing the cell with the fewest remaining candidates to reduce trial and error.

sections.heading: Problem and applicability
paragraphs: Fill periods in a 9×9 board so every row, column, and 3×3 box contains digits 1 through 9 without repetition. Existing digits are fixed constraints and cannot change during search. The interface below copies input and returns one solution, or None for an unsatisfiable board or conflicting initial constraints, allowing independent testing without modifying the caller’s board.

sections.heading: State and key invariants
paragraphs: Maintain nine row sets, column sets, and box sets. Cell (r,c) belongs to box (r//3)*3+c//3. Its available digits are 1..9 minus the union of its three used sets. Every set must match the current board. Placing a digit requires synchronized updates, and failed attempts require synchronized undo operations.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: Each time, choose the remaining empty cell with the fewest candidates: the minimum remaining values strategy. A cell with no candidate makes the branch fail immediately. Prioritizing a cell with just one candidate often triggers more forced choices. This only changes search order without removing valid digits, so completeness is preserved. Return success when all empty cells are filled.

Choices are not undone after success because the function returns the first complete solution rather than enumerating every solution. If the task changes to listing all Sudoku solutions, successful nodes must also record copies and continue restoring state. The Boolean return interface and termination behavior would need corresponding changes.

sections.heading: Implementation details and decisions
paragraphs: To avoid repeatedly copying the empty-cell list, swap the selected cell into the current position and swap it back on return. Once a solution is found, return directly along the successful path without undoing the finished board. Check duplicate fixed digits during initialization so an invalid board is not mistaken for a solved board. The general upper bound remains exponential; a heuristic does not guarantee polynomial time.

space: O(m+81) auxiliary space, including the board copy and recursion stack

paragraphs: An itinerary consumes edges rather than airports. Queens occupy columns and diagonals, not just board cells. Sudoku occupies digits within each row, column, and box. title: Greedy Algorithms: Proving a Local Choice Can Be Retained
summary: A greedy algorithm needs justified irreversible choices, rather than simply taking the largest-looking value at every step.

sections.heading: Understanding the objective and boundaries
paragraphs: A greedy algorithm processes input in an order and makes choices without backtracking. Problems it solves efficiently have useful structure: a current choice can belong to some optimal solution, and the remainder is still the same kind of problem. There is no universal meaning of locally best: it may mean earliest finish, least consumption, farthest coverage, or temporarily making no decision.

sections.heading: Local choice and invariants
paragraphs: Common proofs use exchange arguments and boundary invariants. An exchange argument starts with an optimal solution, replaces its first choice with the greedy choice, and proves the result is no worse. A boundary invariant states that after processing the current prefix, the algorithm retains enough information to represent the future, such as the farthest reachable position or the farthest boundary of all possible landing positions after the current number of jumps.

sections.heading: Why the choice is safe
paragraphs: To find a strategy, identify the final optimization objective, then compare how two local choices affect later possibilities. Earlier-ending intervals leave more time for the future. Giving small cookies to small appetites preserves large cookies for larger demands. If a choice also harms another independent metric, sorting and staged processing or a richer state are often needed.

As an exercise, enumerate optimal retained sets for small inputs containing at most four intervals, then compare them with the earliest-finish strategy. If a counterexample appears, determine whether the strategy is wrong or the endpoint convention differs. Finding no counterexample still does not replace an exchange argument that generalizes the result.

sections.heading: Python implementation notes
paragraphs: The interval scheduling template below selects the largest number of mutually nonoverlapping half-open intervals, allowing touching endpoints. Sort by finish time and always choose the first interval that fits afterward. Every choice leaves an ending boundary no later than alternative choices, so an exchange does not reduce remaining candidates. Half-open endpoint rules are part of input semantics; closed intervals require a different compatibility condition.

space: O(n) for the sorted copy, excluding output

title: 455. Assign Cookies
summary: Use the smallest cookie that satisfies the smallest unmet appetite, preserving larger resources for later.

sections.heading: Understanding the objective and boundaries
paragraphs: Each child may receive at most one cookie, and its size must be at least the child’s appetite. Maximize the number of satisfied children. There is no requirement to maximize what a particular child eats or distribute every cookie. Sort appetites and cookies in ascending order, then compare small demands with small resources using two pointers.

sections.heading: Local choice and invariants
paragraphs: The pointer child identifies the smallest unmet appetite. Process cookies from smallest to largest. Skip a cookie that is too small: if it cannot satisfy the smallest remaining appetite, it cannot satisfy later children. Otherwise, give it to the current child and advance child. After each step, the satisfied count is the maximum achievable with the cookies processed so far.

sections.heading: Why the choice is safe
paragraphs: If an optimal assignment gives the current cookie to a child with a larger appetite, redirect it to the smallest unmet child. If the smaller child already has a cookie, a standard exchange can reassign that cookie without worsening the result. Alternatively, replace a larger demand with the smaller one without reducing the satisfied count. Taking the smallest sufficient resource also preserves larger cookies.

For a rigorous exchange, consider only remaining cookies: the current cookie is the smallest among them. If an optimal assignment gives it to a larger appetite and gives another cookie to the smallest appetite, that other cookie is at least as large and can be exchanged to satisfy the larger appetite. If the smallest appetite was unsatisfied, simply replace the recipient without changing the count.

sections.heading: Python implementation notes
paragraphs: Sort copies to preserve input. Stop once child reaches the end because every child is satisfied. There is no need to rescan cookies for each child; each cookie is checked once. Auxiliary space includes two sorted copies as well as pointers, so this implementation is not O(1) space even though the central scan maintains only constant state.

space: O(g+s) for sorted copies

The second size-1 cookie cannot satisfy the smallest remaining appetite, 2, and is skipped.

pitfalls: A cookie too small for the smallest appetite need not be tried on other children.
The objective is the satisfied count, not total cookie size.

title: 376. Wiggle Subsequence
summary: Changes in the same direction only replace an extreme; increase length only when direction reverses.

sections.heading: Understanding the objective and boundaries
paragraphs: Find the longest subsequence whose adjacent differences alternate strictly between positive and negative. A subsequence may delete elements while preserving order. A zero difference is neither an upward nor a downward step. For input length zero or one, return that length directly. The key question is which endpoint to keep during consecutive changes in one direction, rather than immediately enumerating all subsequences.

sections.heading: Local choice and invariants
paragraphs: prev_sign stores the most recently accepted direction, and count stores the current wiggle length. Ignore zero differences. A difference in the same direction does not increase length; a new direction accepts another turning point and increments length. No subsequence is stored explicitly: a continued rise implicitly replaces its endpoint with a higher peak, and a continued fall with a lower valley.

sections.heading: Why the choice is safe
paragraphs: A higher peak does not obstruct a later fall, and a lower valley does not obstruct a later rise. Intermediate points in one direction can therefore be removed without decreasing the best length. Each direction change is a necessary peak-to-valley or valley-to-peak transition, and the algorithm records exactly these transitions. The first nonzero difference establishes the second element; afterward, length grows only on sign reversals.

For [1,4,7,3], 4 need not be retained. Replacing the rising segment’s endpoint with 7 still permits a fall to 3, giving length three. If the fall reaches only 5, keeping 4 would not allow a downward step. A higher peak thus really does widen the range of later downward choices.

sections.heading: Python implementation notes
paragraphs: Use (diff>0)-(diff<0) to obtain -1, 0, or 1 without a product-based test. Update prev_sign only when accepting a new nonzero direction; resetting it to zero would let a plateau erase existing direction information. This implementation returns length only. To return a subsequence, also store and replace positions of endpoint extremes.

title: 53. Maximum Subarray
summary: A negative prefix only weakens later sums, so restart the current contiguous segment.

sections.heading: Understanding the objective and boundaries
paragraphs: Choose a nonempty contiguous subarray of a nonempty integer array to maximize its sum. Contiguity permits one segment, with no skipping of negative elements inside it. The array may be entirely negative, in which case the answer is its largest individual element. Allowing an empty subarray to return zero would be wrong. The implementation raises an error for empty input to make the nonempty assumption explicit.

sections.heading: Local choice and invariants
paragraphs: current is the maximum subarray sum required to end at the current element. For x, either append x to the previous best ending segment or start with x alone: take max(x,current+x). best stores the largest value among all ending positions processed, so its final value is the global optimum.

sections.heading: Why the choice is safe
paragraphs: A negative previous current only lowers the sum when placed before x, so discard it. A positive current makes extending preferable to taking x alone. This is a greedy explanation based on discarding negative prefixes, and also a one-state dynamic program. One state suffices because any worse prefix with the same endpoint remains worse under an identical future suffix.

For [2,-1,3], the best contiguous segment includes -1 and sums to 4. A negative element is not the same as a negative prefix. Whether to restart depends on the sign of the entire previous current, rather than deleting x whenever it is negative. This example guards against an overly aggressive greedy rule.

sections.heading: Python implementation notes
paragraphs: Initialize both current and best to nums[0] and update from the second item, ensuring a nonempty segment throughout. Do not clamp current to zero and unconditionally update best with zero, which fails for all-negative input. To output endpoints too, record a new start when restarting at x, and record the current end whenever best improves.

title: 122. Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock II
summary: With unlimited transactions, split each rise into positive adjacent gains.

sections.heading: Understanding the objective and boundaries
paragraphs: Given daily prices, make multiple purchases and sales while holding at most one share at any time. Maximize profit. Selling and buying again on one day is allowed because it creates no additional profit. There are no fees, cooldowns, or transaction limits; these assumptions permit splitting rises. Adding any such restriction requires redesigning the algorithm.

sections.heading: Local choice and invariants
paragraphs: Write the profit from buying on day a and selling on day b as a sum of adjacent differences. Every positive difference contributes profit, while every negative difference weakens the holding interval. Summing all positive adjacent rises is therefore equivalent to buying at each rising segment’s valley and selling at its peak.

sections.heading: Why the choice is safe
paragraphs: Any trade’s profit is a segment sum of differences and cannot exceed the sum of positive differences in that segment. Multiple nonoverlapping trades likewise cannot exceed all positive differences across the array. Conversely, one valid purchase and sale can realize the full sum of every contiguous run of positive differences. The upper bound is achievable, proving global optimality.

For the steady rise [1,2,3,4], three adjacent gains of 1 sum to 3, equal to buying at 1 and selling at 4. The accumulation formula does not require actually trading daily; it is simply an easy equivalent profit calculation. Price plateaus contribute nothing and do not interfere with subsequent rises.

sections.heading: Python implementation notes
paragraphs: Start the loop at index 1 and compare each day with the previous one; no explicit holding state is needed. Empty and one-day arrays naturally return zero. Python integers safely accumulate the sum, but real trading costs are outside this problem’s model. Do not apply the strategy directly to stock problems with fees: more splitting may mean more costs.

walkthrough: The rise from 1 to 5 earns 4.
The rise from 3 to 6 earns 3, giving total profit 7.
