title: 55. Jump Game: Maintaining the Farthest Reachable Position
summary: Only reachable positions may extend the coverage boundary.

sections.heading: Understanding the objective and boundaries
paragraphs: nums[i] gives the maximum rightward jump length from index i. Determine whether the last position is reachable from 0. Shorter jumps are allowed, so a reachable position extends a continuous interval. Input is normally nonempty and nonnegative. This implementation defines empty input as unreachable; a single element succeeds without jumping.

sections.heading: Local choice and invariants
paragraphs: far is the farthest index covered by reachable positions processed so far. When scanning i, i>far means i is unreachable, and no known route reaches later positions either, so fail immediately. Otherwise, update with max(far,i+nums[i]). Throughout the scan, every index from 0 through far is reachable.

sections.heading: Why the choice is safe
paragraphs: Use induction. Initially, only 0 is reachable. If i is reachable, any allowed jump length can be chosen, so its new coverage joins the existing reachable prefix without gaps. At the first position beyond far, none of the reachable starting points can cross the boundary. An unreachable position cannot independently initiate another jump.

For [2,0,0], the middle and final positions cannot jump farther, but the start already reaches the end directly, so the answer is true. Seeing zero is not by itself failure. Failure occurs only when the entire reachable prefix cannot extend and the target remains outside it.

sections.heading: Python implementation notes
paragraphs: Return True as soon as far covers the last position; scanning farther is unnecessary. The objective is reachability, not minimum jumps, and far does not describe an actual chosen route. Never update far from an unreachable position, which would incorrectly count an inaccessible large jump as available ability.

time: O(n)

walkthrough: The first three positions cover at most index 3.
Index 3 has jump length zero and cannot cover index 4.

pitfalls: Unreachable positions cannot extend the boundary.
The farthest coverage boundary is not a mandatory landing point for every jump.

title: 45. Jump Game II: Counting Coverage Layers
summary: Treat the entire interval reachable in one jump as a layer, and increment the jump count at layer boundaries.

sections.heading: Understanding the objective and boundaries
paragraphs: Again given maximum rightward jump lengths, find the minimum number of jumps. The original problem guarantees the last position is reachable; this implementation additionally returns -1 for unreachable input. Always jumping to the farthest current landing position is unsafe because a nearer position may offer a stronger next jump. Compare expansions from every reachable landing position in the current layer.

sections.heading: Local choice and invariants
paragraphs: end is the farthest boundary reachable with the current jump count. far is the farthest position reachable with one more jump after scanning positions in the current layer. When i==end, all candidates in this layer have been considered: increment jumps and update end to far. This is breadth-first search with its queue compressed into continuous coverage intervals.

sections.heading: Why the choice is safe
paragraphs: Do not increase jumps before the layer ends, because positions with the same jump count are still being compared. Afterward, any farther position requires at least one additional jump, so incrementing is necessary. The layer’s farthest extension covers every position reachable in one more step and therefore loses no better route.

In the example, the first jump need not land at index 2; the actual optimal route is 0→1→4. Incrementing at boundary 2 only confirms all first-jump candidates have been considered. It does not require landing at 2. Confusing a boundary with a specified landing point misreads the algorithm and yields incorrect routes.

sections.heading: Python implementation notes
paragraphs: Scan only through the second-to-last position: the destination needs no further departure. If far==end, the current layer cannot extend, so return -1 immediately. A single element returns zero, and empty input returns -1. Keep end and far separate; combining them increments jumps prematurely at individual scanned positions.

time: O(n)

walkthrough: The first layer expands from index 0 to 2; the jump count becomes 1.
After scanning 1 and 2, the next layer’s boundary reaches 4; the count becomes 2.

pitfalls: Counting another jump at the last position adds one too many.
Do not select only the farthest current landing point and ignore other positions in the layer.

title: 1005. Maximize Sum of Array After K Negations
summary: Flip the most valuable negative numbers first; spend any remaining odd operation on a minimum-absolute-value item.

sections.heading: Understanding the objective and boundaries
paragraphs: Each operation negates one element. Perform exactly k operations, allowing repeated selection of the same element. Negating a negative increases the sum; negating a positive decreases it. If k is large, two extra operations on the same element cancel completely, leaving only the parity of remaining operations to consider.

sections.heading: Local choice and invariants
paragraphs: Sort by descending absolute value. Negate a negative number while operations remain. More negative values give larger gains, so prioritize greater absolute values. If an odd number of operations remains after processing, one uncancelled negation is necessary. Choose the smallest absolute value to minimize its loss.

sections.heading: Why the choice is safe
paragraphs: Exchange argument: if a plan flips a negative with smaller absolute value but leaves a larger one unflipped, exchanging the operation increases or preserves the sum. Once all negatives have been flipped, pairs of extra operations cancel. An odd count must leave at least one sign reversed, costing at least twice the minimum absolute value; choosing that value achieves the lower bound.

For [-5,-1,2] with k=1, flipping only -5 gives the largest gain. With k=3, both negatives become positive and one operation remains. Flip the absolute-value-1 item, reducing the sum from 8 to 6. This distinguishes the two stages: maximizing gain first and minimizing the final loss.

sections.heading: Python implementation notes
paragraphs: Negation does not change absolute-value ordering, so the final item remains a minimum-absolute-value element. The code creates a copy and explicitly rejects negative k. Empty input is valid only when k=0. Zero is useful: an odd remaining flip on zero has no cost, and the formula handles it naturally without a separate search branch.

time: O(n log n)
space: O(n) for the sorted copy

walkthrough: First turn the larger-absolute-value negative -4 into 4.
Then turn -2 into 2; both operations are used and the sum is 9.

pitfalls: Exactly k operations are required; do not ignore an odd remainder.
The final flip uses minimum absolute value, not minimum numeric value.

title: 134. Gas Station: Eliminating an Entire Failed Interval
summary: When a route segment’s cumulative fuel becomes negative, every starting point in that segment can be discarded.

sections.heading: Understanding the objective and boundaries
paragraphs: On a circular route, station i supplies gas[i] units of fuel, and reaching the next station costs cost[i]. The tank is unlimited and initially empty. Find a starting index that completes one circuit, or return -1. The net gain diff=gas[i]-cost[i] describes fuel gained or lost after that station. A negative total net gain makes a full circuit impossible from every start.

sections.heading: Local choice and invariants
paragraphs: start is the current candidate starting index, and tank is its cumulative net gain through the current station. If tank<0, this start cannot cross the current edge, and neither can any start between start and the current station. Set the next station as the new candidate and reset tank to zero. total independently tracks net gain for the whole circuit.

sections.heading: Why the choice is safe
paragraphs: Why can intermediate starts be eliminated? Before the first failure, cumulative fuel from start to before any intermediate station is nonnegative. Starting at that intermediate station removes a nonnegative reserve, making fuel at the failure point no greater. After scanning, if total≥0, the final candidate follows a minimum prefix, and neither the later segment nor the wrapped earlier segment goes negative.

For net gains [-2,3,-1], the first station fails immediately, making the second station the candidate. It accumulates 3, then has 2 after the third station, and 0 after wrapping to the first, completing the circuit exactly. Zero fuel is permitted: it means no reserve, not failure.

sections.heading: Python implementation notes
paragraphs: Keep local tank separate from global total; changing candidates must not reset total. The code checks that array lengths match and returns -1 for an empty route. Accumulate gains directly without allocating diff to keep auxiliary space constant. The return value is a starting index, not minimum required fuel or total gain.

time: O(n)

walkthrough: Indices 0, 1, and 2 fail in turn, moving the candidate to 3.
Starting at 3 accumulates 3 and then 6; fuel remains nonnegative after wrapping to the earlier segment.

pitfalls: Resetting local fuel must not reset the global total.
tank equal to zero can continue; only a negative value fails.

title: 135. Candy: Deriving Lower Bounds from Both Neighbors
summary: Use two scans for minimum left and right requirements, then take the elementwise maximum.

sections.heading: Understanding the objective and boundaries
paragraphs: Every child receives at least one candy. Of two adjacent children, the higher-rated child must receive more; equal ratings impose no ordering requirement. Minimize total candies. A child may be rated above both neighbors, so a left-to-right scan alone cannot satisfy right-side constraints. Sorting ratings is also invalid because adjacency must be preserved.

sections.heading: Local choice and invariants
paragraphs: Initialize every count to 1. Scan left to right through rating rises: if ratings[i]>ratings[i-1], set candies[i]=candies[i-1]+1. This gives the minimum lower bound when considering only the left side. Then scan right to left to handle right-side requirements caused by descents, using max to preserve the left-side bound already satisfied.

sections.heading: Why the choice is safe
paragraphs: The final count for each child meets requirements from both directions, satisfying every constraint. Any valid allocation must increase along each consecutive rising chain and therefore reach at least the left-scan bound. It must likewise reach the right-side bound along rising chains viewed from the right. Taking the elementwise maximum exactly achieves these necessary bounds, minimizing the sum.

For the mountain [1,2,3,2,1], the left bound is [1,2,3,1,1], and merging the right bound gives [1,2,3,2,1]. A longer descent after the peak may make the right scan raise the peak too. This preserves its requirement to exceed its left neighbor, precisely the purpose of max.

sections.heading: Python implementation notes
paragraphs: Do not overwrite candies[i] directly in the right scan, which could lower a peak and break a left-side relationship. Equal ratings require no increase, so use strict greater-than. Empty input returns zero. Store just one count array and merge during the right scan. More complex slope methods can save space, but two passes are easier to prove and debug.

time: O(n)
space: O(n)

walkthrough: The left scan produces [1,1,2].
The right scan raises the first child’s count to 2, giving [2,1,2].

pitfalls: Equal ratings require neither equal candy counts nor an increase.
Use max in the right scan; do not overwrite a larger left-side requirement.

title: 860. Lemonade Change
summary: For a 20-unit payment, prefer 10+5 in change, preserving flexible 5-unit bills for later customers.

sections.heading: Understanding the objective and boundaries
paragraphs: An item costs 5 units. Customers pay in the given order with 5, 10, or 20, and must receive correct change immediately. Start without change. Customer order cannot change, and future payments cannot be borrowed. Track only counts of 5-unit and 10-unit bills: a 20-unit bill cannot help with later change amounts below 20.

sections.heading: Local choice and invariants
paragraphs: Keep a received 5. A 10 payment consumes one existing 5 and adds one 10. A 20 payment requires 15 in change: prefer one 10 plus one 5, and consider three 5s only if that combination is unavailable. Having enough total money is insufficient; available denominations determine whether the required amount can be made.

sections.heading: Why the choice is safe
paragraphs: Between the two ways to change 20, a 10-unit bill is useful only for changing another 20, while 5-unit bills also serve 10 payments. Spending one 10 and two fewer 5s retains more flexible change. Any successful continuation after using three 5s cannot be worsened by preserving more 5s instead.

Suppose inventory is three 5s and one 10, followed by customers paying 20 and then 10. Giving the first customer three 5s makes the second fail. Using 10+5 leaves two 5s, so the second customer can receive change. This concrete comparison demonstrates the priority rule.

sections.heading: Python implementation notes
paragraphs: Write each denomination branch explicitly and return False immediately upon failure. Unknown denominations return False; an empty queue returns True. The customer’s newly paid 10 cannot supply its own 5 in change: confirm an existing 5 is available before increasing the 10 count.

time: O(n)

walkthrough: The first three customers leave three 5s; after the 10 payment, two 5s and one 10 remain.
Change the 20 with 10+5, leaving one 5.

pitfalls: Tracking only total change value is insufficient.
For a 20 payment, prefer 10+5 over three 5s.

title: 406. Queue Reconstruction by Height
summary: Place taller people first, then insert shorter people at the position matching their required taller-person count.

sections.heading: Understanding the objective and boundaries
paragraphs: A person is represented by [h,k], where h is height and k counts people ahead whose height is at least h. Reconstruct a queue satisfying all conditions. k is neither an original index nor the total number ahead. Inserting at index k has the intended meaning only when everyone already placed is at least as tall as the current person.

sections.heading: Local choice and invariants
paragraphs: Sort by descending height, breaking equal-height ties by ascending k. For the current person, everyone in the queue is at least as tall, so insertion at k puts exactly k qualifying people ahead. Later, shorter people do not count toward this person’s k, so their insertion preserves already-satisfied constraints.

sections.heading: Why the choice is safe
paragraphs: Why sort equal heights by ascending k? Place those requiring fewer qualifying people ahead first, then those requiring more; the later person does not move ahead of an earlier one and increase their count. For height-5 people with k=0 and k=2, handling k=2 first may provide neither enough insertion positions nor the intended prefix-count meaning.

After reconstruction, independently scan each person’s prefix and recount heights at least as large, checking equality with k. This check does not depend on the sorting-and-insertion logic and exposes mistakes in tie sorting or insertion positions. Even a small teaching example should validate every person, rather than queue length alone.

sections.heading: Python implementation notes
paragraphs: Python list.insert(k,p) shifts subsequent elements rightward and is not O(1). Sorting takes O(n log n), while n insertions take O(n²) in the worst case, so insertion dominates. The code copies each record to avoid sharing input sublists in the result. Original-problem input is guaranteed reconstructible; arbitrary external data also needs validation of k ranges and final conditions.

time: O(n²): O(n log n) sorting and O(n²) worst-case total list insertion
space: O(n) for sorted references and the queue

walkthrough: Insert [7,0] and [7,1] first, satisfying constraints among the taller people.
Inserting [5,0] at the front does not affect the 7s’ counts because 5 is shorter than 7.

pitfalls: For equal heights, sort k ascending rather than descending.
list.insert shifts elements; total time cannot be reduced to sorting complexity.

title: 406. Analyzing Insertions: Why Existing People Stay Valid
summary: Analyze how each kind of inserted person affects earlier counts, rather than memorizing a two-key sorting rule.

sections.heading: Understanding the objective and boundaries
paragraphs: This section expands the queue-reconstruction proof. Insertion changes many array indices, but the constraint concerns the number of preceding people at least as tall, rather than indices. An existing element may shift right without its count changing when the newcomer is shorter. Physical movement and constraint changes must be distinguished.

sections.heading: Local choice and invariants
paragraphs: For the current [h,k], the existing queue contains only heights≥h, so index k equals the number of qualifying predecessors. For existing people taller than h, the newcomer does not count. Existing people of height h have k no larger than the current k because of sorting; prove that the current person cannot be inserted ahead of them.

sections.heading: Why the choice is safe
paragraphs: An existing equal-height person was placed at its own k when processed. No taller person arrives afterward, and subsequent equal-height people already processed were inserted at nondecreasing k without invalidating it. The current insertion is therefore after existing equal-height people, so their counts also do not increase. This explains why height sorting alone is insufficient: the secondary key is essential.

For input that cannot be reconstructed, Python insert silently appends when k exceeds list length instead of raising an error. Absence of exceptions is therefore not evidence of successful reconstruction. For general data, an independent valid_queue check is a necessary safeguard for both inputs and results.

sections.heading: Python implementation notes
paragraphs: The example returns a snapshot after every insertion for observation and is unsuitable for large input. Copying each small record in the queue at every step adds O(n²) total copying, the same order as list insertion, but snapshot output itself also takes O(n²). Validate the final result by directly counting qualifying predecessors, independently of construction.

time: O(n²) construction and snapshots; O(n²) independent validation
space: O(n) auxiliary space; O(n²) snapshot output

walkthrough: Place the taller person, 6, first.
Insert [5,0] at the front and [5,1] after it; the 6’s count remains zero.

pitfalls: An array index shifting right does not imply the constrained count increases.
Complete the proof by explaining the processing order for equal heights.

title: 452. Minimum Number of Arrows to Burst Balloons
summary: Place an arrow at the earliest-ending balloon’s right endpoint to also cover later balloons overlapping it.

sections.heading: Understanding the objective and boundaries
paragraphs: Each balloon occupies a closed interval [start,end]. An arrow bursts it if its horizontal coordinate lies inside that interval, and one arrow may burst multiple balloons. Find the fewest arrows covering all intervals. Closed intervals permit endpoint shots: [1,2] and [2,3] can both be burst by one arrow at 2.

sections.heading: Local choice and invariants
paragraphs: Sort by ascending right endpoint. Shoot at the right endpoint of the earliest-ending uncovered balloon and store that position in shot. A later balloon with start≤shot is already covered. If start>shot, a new arrow is necessary; set shot to that balloon’s right endpoint. Sorting ensures later right endpoints are not smaller than shot.

sections.heading: Why the choice is safe
paragraphs: Every solution needs an arrow covering the earliest-ending balloon. Move that arrow rightward to this balloon’s right endpoint. Later balloons it previously covered have right endpoints at least that large and left endpoints no greater than the original shot, so they remain covered. This exchange does not increase the arrow count. Repeat for the remaining uncovered balloons.

There is no need to choose an interval midpoint. Its right endpoint covers the earliest-ending interval while reaching as far right as possible to cover later ones, which is the sorted exchange argument. Sorting by starts and shooting at left endpoints may use an extra arrow for [1,10] and [2,3], losing optimality.

sections.heading: Python implementation notes
paragraphs: Initialize the shot using None or the first item, avoiding floating-point sentinels with large integer endpoints. Empty input returns zero. Add an arrow only for strict greater-than, not greater-than-or-equal: touching balloons can share an arrow. The sorted copy takes O(n) space, while scanning maintains only a position and count.

time: O(n log n)
space: O(n) for sorting and the scan slice

walkthrough: Shoot the first arrow at 6, covering [1,6] and [2,8].
[7,12] is still uncovered; shoot the second at 12, also covering [10,16].

pitfalls: Closed intervals touching at endpoints can share an arrow.
Do not sort by left endpoints and add an arrow for every different interval.

title: 435. Non-overlapping Intervals
summary: Maximize the number of retained intervals, then subtract it from the total.

sections.heading: Understanding the objective and boundaries
paragraphs: Delete the fewest intervals so the rest are pairwise nonoverlapping. Touching endpoints do not count as overlap: [1,2] and [2,3] may both remain. Rewriting minimum deletions as maximum retention gives classic interval scheduling. Its objective differs from balloon bursting; interval-shaped input alone does not justify reusing counting logic.

sections.heading: Local choice and invariants
paragraphs: Process by ascending right endpoint, retaining the first interval and then only intervals starting no earlier than the current end. end is the finish time of the last retained interval. Earlier finishing leaves more room afterward, making the earliest-finishing available interval the best next choice.

sections.heading: Why the choice is safe
paragraphs: If an optimal solution’s first interval is not the earliest-finishing one, replace it with that interval. The new finish is no later and therefore cannot conflict with subsequent intervals. The retained count is unchanged. Apply this exchange repeatedly to compatible remaining intervals. The greedy retained set thus also has maximum cardinality, and deletions equal n-kept.

For duplicate intervals of positive length, at most one can remain; the others must be deleted. With containment, favoring the shorter, earlier-ending inner interval may allow subsequent intervals to begin sooner. Empty input requires zero deletions. Initializing with None handles these boundaries without special cases.

sections.heading: Python implementation notes
paragraphs: Touching endpoints are compatible, so use start>=end. Initialize end=None for the first item rather than an integer that might conflict with the input range. This code returns the minimum count rather than specific deleted indices. To return the retained set, record intervals in the retain branch; the proof is unchanged.

time: O(n log n)
space: O(n) for the sorted copy

walkthrough: Retain [1,2], then [2,3].
Skip conflicting [1,3]; [3,4] fits next, leaving three retained intervals.

pitfalls: Touching is compatible here, unlike the shared-point semantics of closed intervals.
Return the deletion count, not kept directly.

title: 763. Partition Labels
summary: A segment may close only after every character it contains has reached its final occurrence.

sections.heading: Understanding the objective and boundaries
paragraphs: Partition a string into as many contiguous segments as possible so each character occurs in only one segment, and return segment lengths. Even distant occurrences of one character connect all intervening positions into the same segment. The goal is not evenly sized segments, but finishing each segment as early as its constraints allow.

sections.heading: Local choice and invariants
paragraphs: First record each character’s last position in last. While scanning a segment, maintain end=max(end,last[c]), its minimum required ending position to include every character seen so far. A newly encountered character may extend this boundary farther right. Cut only when the current i==end.

sections.heading: Why the choice is safe
paragraphs: Cutting before end leaves some already-seen character appearing again at end or another future position up to end, violating the one-segment-per-character rule. At i==end, no character in the current segment appears later, so the cut is safe. Taking the earliest safe cut maximizes segment count without restricting later valid partitions.

For abac, the first a sets the boundary to index 2. Although b last occurs at 1, it must not shrink the boundary. Cut aba after the second a, leaving c alone. This small example checks both max and cut timing.

sections.heading: Python implementation notes
paragraphs: Store the segment’s starting index in start and calculate length as i-start+1. After a cut, set start=i+1. Characters need not be lowercase letters: a dictionary supports arbitrary string characters, with space determined by the distinct character count. Empty input naturally returns an empty list. Do not cut merely when one character reaches its own final position; check the whole segment’s maximum boundary.

time: O(n)
space: O(σ) auxiliary space, where σ is the distinct character count, excluding output

walkthrough: The first segment contains a, b, and c; their final positions push its boundary to 8.
It can close only at index 8, giving length 9.

pitfalls: Maintain the maximum final position among all characters in the segment.
Add one when calculating a closed interval’s length.

title: 56. Merge Intervals
summary: After sorting by left endpoint, decide only whether the next interval extends the current merged segment.

sections.heading: Understanding the objective and boundaries
paragraphs: Given closed intervals, merge every overlap and return nonoverlapping intervals covering exactly the same set. For example, [1,3] and [3,5] share an endpoint and merge to [1,5]. This task retains all covered positions while reducing the number of interval representations, rather than selecting or deleting some intervals.

sections.heading: Local choice and invariants
paragraphs: Scan by ascending left endpoint. The final segment in result is the rightmost merged segment so far. If the next start exceeds that segment’s right endpoint, there is a gap, so create a new segment. Otherwise they overlap or touch; set the right endpoint to max(previous right endpoint,end). Earlier completed segments never need modification again.

sections.heading: Why the choice is safe
paragraphs: Sorting prevents future starts from moving left. If a gap separates the current interval from the last segment, no later interval with an even larger start can fill it, so the earlier segment is final. If they overlap, their union is still one interval from the smaller left endpoint to the larger right endpoint. Updating preserves equivalent coverage.

Sorting ensures increasing left endpoints, not increasing right endpoints. Thus [1,10] followed by [2,3] must retain 10. Replacing the right endpoint with the current end loses coverage from 4 through 10. Containment tests reveal this shortening error more readily than crossing overlaps alone.

sections.heading: Python implementation notes
paragraphs: Create a new list for each merged segment instead of modifying input interval objects. Comparing only neighboring original intervals is insufficient: a long interval may contain multiple short ones. Always compare with the latest merged right endpoint. Empty input returns an empty list. Adjust conditions if semantics change to open intervals or prohibit merging touching intervals.

time: O(n log n)
space: O(n) for the sorted copy; at most O(n) output

walkthrough: [2,6] overlaps [1,3], extending the current right endpoint to 6.
8 exceeds 6, leaving a gap, so start another segment.

pitfalls: Update right endpoints with max so long intervals never shrink.
Closed intervals sharing an endpoint must merge here.

title: 738. Monotone Increasing Digits
summary: When adjacent digits descend, decrease the left digit and maximize the affected suffix with 9s.

sections.heading: Understanding the objective and boundaries
paragraphs: Find the largest integer no greater than nonnegative n whose decimal digits are nondecreasing from left to right. Equal digits are allowed, as in 1123. Trying each number below n is too slow for large inputs. Determine which higher digit must decrease and, once it does, how to maximize the lower digits afterward.

sections.heading: Local choice and invariants
paragraphs: Convert the number to a character list and inspect adjacent digits from right to left. If digits[i-1]>digits[i], the higher digit is too large: decrement it and record that the suffix from i onward must become all 9s. Right-to-left traversal handles cascading changes. For 332, decrementing its second digit to 2 makes the first 3 too large as well, requiring another step left.

sections.heading: Why the choice is safe
paragraphs: Once a higher digit changes, the result is strictly smaller than the original number, so all digits to its right can be maximized. Filling them with 9 gives the largest suffix and is compatible with preceding digits no greater than 9. If an earlier inversion appears, move the change point left. The final leftmost decremented digit incurs the smallest necessary loss in higher places, with the 9 suffix maximizing the rest.

For 120, the final 0 makes the middle 2 decrease to 1. The first two digits become 11, and filling the suffix with 9 gives 119; the first digit need not decrease. For 1110, decrements cascade to the leading digit, producing 999. Comparing these checks whether mark moves left throughout a cascade.

sections.heading: Python implementation notes
paragraphs: mark stores the earliest position requiring 9s. Fill the suffix only after scanning, so early 9s do not mask cascading conflicts. Single-digit character comparisons agree with numeric comparisons; use int when decrementing. For example, 1000 becomes 0999, and the final int conversion removes the leading zero to yield 999.

time: O(d), where d is the decimal digit count, using the usual linear-cost integer-conversion model
space: O(d)

walkthrough: On the right, 3>2: decrement the middle 3 to 2 and set mark=2.
On the left, 3>2 again: decrement it to 2, set mark=1, and fill the suffix with 9s.

pitfalls: Check right to left to propagate inversions after a decrement.
Fill 9s only at the end, avoiding premature masking of conflicts.

title: 968. Binary Tree Cameras: Three States in Postorder
summary: Place a camera at a parent when a child is uncovered, positioning devices to cover more relationships.

sections.heading: Understanding the objective and boundaries
paragraphs: A camera covers its own node, its parent, and its immediate children. Find the fewest cameras covering the entire binary tree. A tree has no cycles, allowing child subtrees to be processed first. Installing at bottom-level leaves is usually undesirable because a camera on a leaf’s parent can also cover siblings and its own parent. Use bottom-up state decisions.

sections.heading: Local choice and invariants
paragraphs: The postorder function returns three states: 0 means the current node is uncovered; 1 means it has a camera; 2 means it is covered by a child’s camera but has no camera itself. A null node returns 2: it needs no device and must not force a leaf to install one. Increment the camera count whenever state 1 is created.

sections.heading: Why the choice is safe
paragraphs: If either child returns 0, place a camera at the current node to cover it. This is no worse than putting the camera on that child and can additionally cover the other child and the current node’s parent. Otherwise, if either child has a camera, the current node is covered and returns 2. If both children are merely covered, nobody covers the current node; return 0 and leave it for its parent.

A three-node chain needs only one camera on the middle node, while an isolated root needs one camera of its own. The former checks the benefit of covering a child and the camera node’s parent; the latter checks root completion. Returning uncovered for null nodes incorrectly forces every leaf to install a camera, inflating the count.

sections.heading: Python implementation notes
paragraphs: The root has no parent, so add a camera if its final state is 0. The code includes an independent TreeNode definition and a level-order construction helper. An empty tree returns zero. Postorder recursion depth is tree height h, reaching O(n) for a degenerate chain; do not simply write O(log n). States describe coverage relationships, not an array of minimum counts, so distinguish return states from the count.

time: O(n); the tree-construction helper additionally takes O(n)
space: O(h) solver recursion, where h is tree height; O(n) for the construction helper

walkthrough: Both leaves are uncovered, forcing their parent to install a camera.
The root is covered by its child’s camera and needs no extra device.

pitfalls: Treat null nodes as needing no coverage, rather than uncovered.
Add a final camera if the root returns uncovered.
Evaluate the three states by checking for uncovered children first.

title: Checkpoint: Matching, Peaks and Valleys, and Positive Gains
summary: When local gains decompose, identify choices that weaken the future and prove that removing them preserves optimality.

sections.heading: Identify the problem structure
paragraphs: 455 preserves larger cookies in resource matching; 376 keeps more extreme endpoints during one-direction changes; 53 discards a negative accumulated prefix; 122 excludes negative differences during holding periods. All reduce unfavorable choices, but compare different things: demand size, room for future reversals, contiguous segment sums, and adjacent trading gains. Derive each strategy from its own objective instead of memorizing “delete bad elements.”

sections.heading: Compare local choices
paragraphs: Maximum subarrays must be contiguous, so a negative number is not necessarily removable. While the prefix sum remains positive, a negative may be a necessary bridge to a later large positive. Unlimited stock trading allows selling before a drop, so every negative difference can be avoided. Applying both problems to the same numeric array shows how constraints change the removable unit; the answers should not be expected to match.

sections.heading: Proof and boundary checks
paragraphs: Same-direction runs can be compressed in wiggle subsequences, but zero differences add no wiggle. Undersized resources can be skipped in cookie matching, but giving away large resources earlier is not inherently better. Test all-negative and all-equal arrays, decreasing prices, and wholly insufficient resources. Check that state retains the original nonempty or validity requirements and that the objective has not silently changed.

sections.heading: Implementation and practice
paragraphs: The maximum-subarray implementation below uses an index loop without slicing, making auxiliary solver space truly constant. current is the best sum ending at the current position; best is the best over all processed endpoints. Write both values for every example item, especially at -3 and 4, to see why the prefix can be discarded. Verify all-negative input still chooses one element. Recovering the actual subarray also requires recording restart indices.

time: O(n) for the example; matching additionally includes sorting
space: O(1) for the example

walkthrough: After the first three items, best remains 1 and the current ending sum is -2.
Restart at 4, then append -1 and 2 to obtain 5.

title: Checkpoint: Reachability Boundaries, Layer Boundaries, and Failed Intervals
summary: When intervals represent many candidates, distinguish boundaries representing ability from those representing cost.

sections.heading: Identify the problem structure
paragraphs: In 55, far is the farthest coverage of all processed reachable positions, not a mandatory landing point. 45 additionally needs end as the boundary for a fixed jump count and far as the next layer’s possible boundary. Both compress continuous reachable sets, but only the latter increments cost when changing layers. A single variable for every boundary is confusing; first draw the index interval covered by each layer.

sections.heading: Compare local choices
paragraphs: 134 also eliminates a batch of starting candidates through a failed interval, but uses cumulative net gain rather than geometric distance. Prefix sums before the first failure are nonnegative; removing such a reserve cannot make an intermediate start succeed. Efficiency comes from a local conclusion applying to an entire candidate batch, rather than arbitrary loop skipping. Explain why the whole batch is equivalent or fails: this is the core of the complexity reduction.

sections.heading: Proof and boundary checks
paragraphs: 1005 compresses surplus operations by parity: negating the same item twice cancels, leaving only an odd-operation loss to consider. Both boundary and operation compression require discarded information to be irrelevant to future decisions. Transaction fees in stocks, backward jumps, or a limited fuel tank may make the original state insufficient. Reprove the compression: even a small-looking constraint change can invalidate it.

title: Checkpoint: Two-Sided Constraints and Resource Denominations
summary: When a local choice affects two directions or resource types, separate the necessary constraints first.

sections.heading: Identify the problem structure
paragraphs: 135’s rating relationships come from both neighbors, and one pass satisfies only one side. Each direction supplies a necessary candy lower bound; their maximum satisfies both without exceeding minimum needs. In 406, height and preceding counts interact. Descending heights first fixes who counts, then insertion by k avoids blindly adjusting two dimensions simultaneously. Both solve one direction or dimension first and preserve that progress.

sections.heading: Compare local choices
paragraphs: 860’s change consists of resources with different denominations. A 5-unit bill serves two kinds of change requests; a 10 primarily serves 20 payments. Spending less flexible resources first preserves more flexible ones, which is why 10+5 beats three 5s. Tracking only total value loses feasibility information: enough money may still fail to make exact change. Even a constant-size state must cover all important resource types.

sections.heading: Proof and boundary checks
paragraphs: Compare these strategies by asking whether the current action breaks completed conditions. Candy’s right scan uses max to preserve the left lower bound. A newly inserted shorter person leaves taller people’s counts unchanged. Preferred change preserves more 5-unit bills. Proof concerns future possibilities or already-satisfied relationships, rather than a universal notion of numeric size. When two actions are feasible, compare their effects on the future.

title: Checkpoint: Distinguish Interval Objectives and Endpoint Rules
summary: Arrow shooting, selection, and merging share sorting tools but give boundaries and endpoint comparisons different meanings.

sections.heading: Identify the problem structure
paragraphs: 452 covers every closed interval with points: place arrows by ending time, and a start equal to the shot is still covered. 435 retains as many nonconflicting intervals as possible: earliest finishes leave future room, and touching intervals may coexist. 56 retains all coverage: sort by start, extend the current right endpoint, and merge touching intervals. Different objectives directly determine sorting and state.

sections.heading: Compare local choices
paragraphs: All compare start with end, but 452 adds an arrow when start>end; 435 retains an interval when start>=end; 56 creates a merged segment when start>end. The extra equality is a problem-definition issue, not coding style. Before coding, work out [1,2] and [2,3] manually, then translate the result into a comparison, reducing boundary errors from memorized formulas.

sections.heading: Proof and boundary checks
paragraphs: 763 can be viewed as implicitly merging intervals between each character’s first and last positions. Characters encountered during scanning push the segment end farther right until every dependency closes. Explicit generation and sorting of character intervals is unnecessary because string traversal naturally advances by first involvement. This connection clarifies boundaries but does not replace the proof that characters never span segments, especially when new characters appear later within a segment.

title: Greedy Algorithms Summary: Strategies, Proofs, and Counterexamples
summary: Every greedy solution should justify its choice, sufficient state, and preservation of optimal answers.

sections.heading: Identify the problem structure
paragraphs: First identify the objective and constraints: maximum satisfied count, maximum profit, minimum jumps, minimum interval deletions, minimum devices, and so on. Similar input does not imply the same strategy. Balloon arrows and interval scheduling both sort by endings but maintain a coverage point and a previous finish time, respectively. State the objective in one sentence to identify necessary information and avoid calling a merely feasible solution optimal.

sections.heading: Compare local choices
paragraphs: Next propose a local choice and seek a proof. Cookies, earliest-finishing intervals, and change suit exchange arguments. Jumping suits reachable-prefix and layer-boundary invariants. Gas stations eliminate failed intervals. Candy uses necessary lower bounds. Tree cameras use coverage states and parent-child relationships. If only intuition is available and replacements or boundaries cannot be explained, retain the strategy as a conjecture and seek small counterexamples before writing complex code.

sections.heading: Proof and boundary checks
paragraphs: 738 discovers inversions from lower digits and propagates decreases toward higher digits, reflecting that higher places determine numeric order first. 968 handles uncovered nodes upward from subtrees, reflecting cameras’ local coverage structure. Greedy algorithms need not scan left to right or sort. Processing order must provide all information needed for a current decision; derive traversal direction and state definition together.

sections.heading: Implementation and practice
paragraphs: Finally, test conjectures with small exhaustive searches or independent constraint checkers, focusing on equal values, all-negative numbers, touching boundaries, unreachability, and root-specific cases. The interval selector below returns a concrete set, making it possible to inspect why every exchange preserves optimal cardinality. Tests expose mistakes, but general correctness still requires reasoning for arbitrary input. Include sorting, list movement, and output copying in time analysis.
